conflictGroups.why: Same mechanism: an agent output item is linked to its request by the item-level id (call_id, or the mcp_approval_request item id), never by response.id. True s2.2-09 teaches the item-level pattern, so false s2.2-10 (uses response.id) becomes easy.

conflictGroups.name: id-not-position-correlation
conflictGroups.why: Both are false through the same 'outputs are paired with inputs by position' claim: Batch output order versus custom_id, and Custom Web API skill array position versus recordId. Seeing one explanation answers the other.

conflictGroups.name: responses-api-model-routing
conflictGroups.why: Both teach 'this model feature needs the Responses API, not Chat Completions'. The s1.1-10 explanation (gpt-5.1-codex uses the Responses API, a Chat Completions app needs a compatible model) and the s2.3-05 explanation (Chat Completions tool calls need reasoning_effort none) each hint the other answer.

conflictGroups.name: gpt56-reasoning-controls
conflictGroups.why: The s2.3-05 explanation names reasoning_effort as the separate reasoning control. That gives away s2.3-02 (false: text.verbosity controls reasoning effort).

conflictGroups.name: vision-capable-deployment
conflictGroups.why: The statements of s3.2-01 and s3.2-03 both say 'vision-capable model(s)', which presents image understanding as a property of the model deployment. That hints s1.1-06 is false (a Foundry connection adds image understanding).

conflictGroups.name: responses-image-input-parts
conflictGroups.why: Both are true and close together. One message carries input_text plus input_image content parts, and several images go in one request. Knowing the content-part model makes the multi-image card obvious, and the reverse.

conflictGroups.name: file-search-ingestion
conflictGroups.why: The s1.1-01 explanation ('chunks uploaded files during managed ingestion') presents ingestion as a step separate from upload. That hints s2.2-05 is false (the upload response confirms ingestion has finished).

conflictGroups.name: code-interpreter-sandbox
conflictGroups.why: The s1.1-03 explanation stresses a 'managed sandbox' that analyzes 'attached data files'. That points toward s2.2-06 being false (the sandbox fetches public web pages).

conflictGroups.name: rag-vs-finetune-grounding
conflictGroups.why: The s1.1-08 explanation ('RAG retrieves changing records for grounding') answers s2.1-03 (a RAG app passes retrieved passages into generation), which is already close to the definition of RAG.

conflictGroups.name: prompt-agent-tracing
conflictGroups.why: The s2.3-07 statement and explanation show tool-execution spans inside prompt-agent traces. That strongly suggests s1.4-09 is true (traces capture tool-call arguments).

conflictGroups.name: foundry-project-endpoint
conflictGroups.why: Both test what the Foundry project endpoint is for. The s1.2-08 explanation contrasts the project endpoint with the direct Azure OpenAI endpoint, and the s1.2-07 statement establishes the project endpoint's role. In one round each frames the other.

conflictGroups.name: openai-v1-client-config
conflictGroups.why: s1.2-05 shows base_url ending in /openai/v1/, with the version in the path. That hints s1.2-04 is false (a dated api-version is still required).

conflictGroups.name: gpt-image-jpeg-output
conflictGroups.why: The s3.1-04 explanation ('output_compression applies to JPEG output') confirms JPEG output, which answers s3.1-03 (output_format jpeg). The s3.1-03 statement in turn makes JPEG the obvious target for compression in s3.1-04.

conflictGroups.name: gpt-image-edit-inputs
conflictGroups.why: s3.1-09 (input_fidelity preserves faces 'in a GPT-Image-2 edit') and s3.1-06 (mask marks 'an edit target') both assume that GPT-Image-2 edits take a supplied image. That gives away s3.1-01 (a reference image can be passed for an edit).

conflictGroups.name: content-credentials-scope
conflictGroups.why: Three provenance cards. The s3.3-08 explanation ('disclose origin ... do not establish whether an image contains harmful content') and the s3.3-07 explanation (signed provenance metadata, tamper check) define the scope of credentials, which answers s3.3-09 (proves who prompted). s3.3-08 and s3.3-09 also share one false template.

conflictGroups.name: image-safety-category-scores
conflictGroups.why: The s3.3-02 explanation lists the fixed categories, including Sexual and Violence. The s3.3-05 explanation says image:analyze returns per-category severity scores and the app decides. Together these answer s3.3-03 (several categories reported for one image). The s3.3-03 explanation ('the app handles simultaneous detections') hints s3.3-05 is false.

conflictGroups.name: cu-video-segment-fields
conflictGroups.why: The s3.2-07 statement shows Content Understanding returning video schema fields, which gives away s1.1-05 (select Content Understanding for schema-shaped video metadata). The s3.2-07 explanation ('a segmented video result') and s3.2-05 (enableSegment:false) frame each other as the two segmentation modes.

conflictGroups.name: cu-field-source-confidence
conflictGroups.why: The s5.2-08 explanation names estimateFieldSourceAndConfidence and estimateSourceAndConfidence. These options show that source grounding is a field-level output, which primes s5.2-07 (read the field's source string), and s5.2-07 in turn suggests source and confidence are configured features.

conflictGroups.name: semantic-ranker-scope
conflictGroups.why: Both are false because they give the semantic ranker more than reordering and extraction (fetching missed documents, writing new answer text). Each explanation ('reorders documents supplied by initial retrieval', 'extract verbatim passages') answers the other.

conflictGroups.name: translator-style-controls
conflictGroups.why: The s4.1-03 statement shows that tone and style control comes from LLM translation's tone parameter. That hints s4.1-06 is false (category works as a writing-style prompt).

conflictGroups.name: custom-speech-endpoint-vs-model
conflictGroups.why: These are the two sides of one distinction: a deployed custom endpoint (endpoint_id) for real-time recognition versus the custom model URI (model.self) for batch transcription. The s4.2-08 explanation ('a deployed recognition endpoint identifies a different resource') hints s4.2-06.

conflictGroups.name: realtime-input-buffer
conflictGroups.why: The s4.2-10 statement exposes the input_audio_buffer.* event family, which makes the input_audio_buffer.append name in s4.2-09 easy to accept. The s4.2-09 explanation in turn frames the buffer as input-only, which hints s4.2-10 is false (commit starts a response).

scan.tells:
All 140 cards read, 70 true and 70 false, 5/5 in every section. Length is not a tell: true and false means are within 5 characters in every section (largest gaps 4.6 in 3.2 and 3.3, 4.2 in 1.3 and 4.2, 4.0 in 5.1 and 5.2), and explanations average 134 characters for true cards and 136 for false.

1) Subject framing (strongest tell). When the subject is the developer or the app ('An engineer/A developer/An app/A ... app ...'), the card is true 35 times and false 19 times. When the subject is the service or a feature ('Azure ...', 'Foundry ...', 'Microsoft ...', 'Content Understanding ...', 'GPT-Image-2's ...', 'Grounding ...', 'Code Interpreter ...'), it is false about 37 times and true about 20 times. Rule of thumb: 'the developer does X' means true, 'the service does X' means false.

2) Verbs that mark true:
- 'sets': 4 true, 0 false (s1.2-05, s3.1-09, s3.2-05, s4.2-06)
- 'lets': 4 true, 0 false (s1.3-04, s2.2-03, s2.2-07, s2.3-07). The rule asks hedge verbs to be balanced.
- 'selects/chooses': 9 true (s1.1-01, s1.1-03, s1.1-05, s1.1-09, s2.2-04, s3.1-03, s3.1-07, s4.1-03, s4.2-02), 2 false (s1.1-08, s1.1-10)
- 'reads': 4 true (s2.3-09, s3.2-09, s4.2-04, s4.2-05), 1 false (s4.1-04)

3) Verbs that mark false:
- 'uses': 4 true, 9 false (false: s1.2-06, s1.3-03, s1.4-03, s2.1-06, s2.2-02, s2.2-10, s3.3-04, s4.1-06, s5.1-02)
- confirmation verbs (confirms/confirmation/proves/validates): 0 true, 6 false (s1.3-05, s1.4-03, s2.1-04, s2.2-02, s2.2-05, s3.3-09)
- 'treats/treat ... as': 0 true, 3 false (s2.2-05, s3.3-08, s5.1-08)
- 'own': 0 true, 3 false (s1.1-02, s1.2-10, s2.1-10)
- 'rejects': 0 true, 2 false (s2.1-10, s3.1-08). These work as hidden negations.
- 'returns': 2 true, 4 false
'can' is roughly balanced (11 true, 14 false), and 'by default/automatically' is balanced (true s2.2-08, s5.2-01; false s5.2-08, s2.2-01).

4) Recurring false templates (rule: at most 2 per deck):
(a) 'a status/annotation/response/credential confirms or proves Y': s1.3-05, s1.4-03, s2.2-05, s3.3-08, s3.3-09. That is 5, over the limit.
(b) 'feature X can also do neighbouring job Y': s1.1-06, s3.3-02, s4.1-06, s4.1-08, s5.1-02, s5.1-03, s5.2-10. That is 7, all false.
(c) 'parameter A controls B's job': s2.3-02 (verbosity to reasoning), s3.2-04 (detail to output-token limit), s3.1-04 (compression to PNG). That is 3, over the limit.
(d) 'outputs paired by position instead of id': s2.1-08, s5.1-06. That is 2, at the limit, and it echoes the id-association cards s2.2-09 and s2.2-10.
(e) 'the API resolves a conflict or precedence in favour of X': s3.3-04, s4.2-07. That is 2, at the limit.

5) Section 3.1 pattern: all 5 true statements start with 'The app', and the 3 statements that do not start with 'The app' are all false (s3.1-04, s3.1-08, s3.1-10). Inside this section, sentence shape predicts the answer. 3.1 statements (about 82 characters) and explanations (about 62 characters) are also much shorter than in the rest of the deck. That is a style break, not an answer tell.

6) Difficulty skew: difficulty-3 cards are 18 false and 10 true, so a 'hard means false' bias exists if difficulty is shown to the player.

7) Weak cards: s3.1-01 is near a truism (an image edit takes a reference image), s2.1-03 restates the definition of RAG, and s3.3-08 is near a strawman (provenance treated as a safety pass).

Spot-checks against Microsoft Learn (fetched 2026-10-13) confirm s1.1-02 (developers have no access to raw Bing grounding content), s2.2-01 and s2.2-09 (the app executes the function and returns function_call_output with call_id), and s3.1-02, s3.1-04, s3.1-06, s3.1-08, s3.1-09 and s3.1-10 (GPT-Image-2 outputs base64 only; output_compression is JPEG-only; masks use transparent pixels; edits accept PNG or JPG; input_fidelity preserves faces; size constraints apply only when a size is given).

source.title: Default safety policies in Microsoft Foundry
How to configure guardrails and controls in Microsoft Foundry
Use the Azure OpenAI Responses API

rewrite.reason: weak_card (name giveaway). Rewrite needed to keep 1.1 at 9 cards; verifier replacement confirmed.
rewrite.statement: A Foundry agent's Code Interpreter sandbox runs in the same Azure region as the agent's Foundry project.
rewrite.explanation: Code Interpreter runs in Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions placed in the Foundry project's own region, which matters when an engineer plans for data residency.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Use Code Interpreter with Microsoft Foundry agents

rewrite.reason: weak_card (strawman, unsupported explanation). Rewrite needed to keep 1.1 at 9 cards; Phi-4-mini-instruct 'Input: text' and Phi-4-multimodal-instruct 'text, images, and audio' confirmed.
rewrite.statement: An engineer selects Phi-4-mini-instruct as a small language model for captioning product photos.
rewrite.explanation: Phi-4-mini-instruct accepts text input only. Phi-4-multimodal-instruct is the Phi-4 option that accepts text, images and audio.
rewrite.misconception: Every small Phi-4 chat model can read image input.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Foundry Models from partners and community

rewrite.reason: weak_card (name giveaway). Rewrite needed to keep 1.2 at 9 cards with 4T/5F. Troubleshooting row 'No PTU capacity in region | ... use Global Provisioned for broader availability' confirmed; set volatility may_change.
rewrite.statement: When a region lacks PTU capacity for Regional Provisioned, an engineer deploys Global Provisioned instead.
rewrite.explanation: Global Provisioned reserves PTUs on Azure's global infrastructure, so Microsoft suggests it when regional PTU capacity is unavailable and global processing is acceptable.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Understanding deployment types in Microsoft Foundry Models

rewrite.reason: explanation_error: the card described renaming an existing deployment, which is undocumented. Per the source, the name is chosen before deploying and is used in the model parameter. appliesTo becomes empty because the source states this for Foundry Models in general.
rewrite.statement: An app puts the catalog model name in the model parameter to call a deployment that has a custom name.
rewrite.explanation: During inference, the model parameter carries the deployment name. A deployment given a custom name at creation is called by that name, not by the catalog model name.
rewrite.misconception: The catalog model name routes to a deployment whatever the deployment is named.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Deploy Microsoft Foundry Models in the Foundry portal

rewrite.reason: weak_card (truism). Rewrite needed to keep 1.2 balanced. 'Each version of an agent is immutable after you save it' and '<agent_name>:<version>' confirmed.
rewrite.statement: In Foundry Agents v2, a developer who changes a saved agent version's instructions creates a new agent version.
rewrite.explanation: Saved Foundry agent versions are immutable, so any change is saved as a new version. Code refers to an agent as <agent_name>:<version>.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Agent development lifecycle in Microsoft Foundry

rewrite.reason: tell: removes 'lets' (4 true / 0 false in the scan) and the engineer-subject framing. Fact and answer unchanged; original explanation kept.
rewrite.statement: Azure Monitor splits Azure OpenAI's blocked-request metric by the content category behind each block.
rewrite.explanation: The Blocked Volume metric counts Azure OpenAI requests rejected by content filters. Its Category dimension helps an engineer identify the categories causing rejections.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Monitoring data reference for Azure OpenAI

rewrite.reason: weak_card (near-truism, near-copy). Rewrite needed to keep 1.3 at 9 cards. 'An indexer run can be successful even if individual documents have errors, if the number of errors is less than the indexer's Max failed items setting' confirmed.
rewrite.statement: An Azure AI Search indexer run can report success while some documents in that run failed to index.
rewrite.explanation: A run still counts as successful while its document errors stay below the indexer's Max failed items setting, so an engineer checks a run's errors even after success.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Monitor indexer status and results

rewrite.reason: weak_card (role-name giveaway). Rewrite needed to keep 1.3 at 9 cards. Permissions table shows Publish agents as an X for Foundry User; 'To publish agents, you need the Foundry Project Manager role (minimum) on the Foundry resource scope' confirmed.
rewrite.statement: Foundry User on a Foundry resource gives a developer permission to publish agents from its projects.
rewrite.explanation: Foundry User covers building and testing agents in a project. Publishing agents needs at least Foundry Project Manager at the Foundry resource scope.
rewrite.misconception: The developer role for building agents also covers publishing them.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Role-based access control for Microsoft Foundry

rewrite.reason: weak_card (flipped source sentence; 'legacy' tell). Rewrite needed to keep 1.3 at 9 cards. Time to Response is 'as measured by the API gateway' and 'does not account for any client-side latency' (confirmed).
rewrite.statement: Azure OpenAI's Time to Response metric includes network latency between the client app and the API endpoint.
rewrite.explanation: Time to Response is measured at the API gateway up to the first response, so client-side network latency is outside it. End-to-end timing comes from the app's own logging.
rewrite.misconception: Service-side latency metrics capture the client's full round trip.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Monitoring data reference for Azure OpenAI

rewrite.reason: weak_card (wrong actor, two reasons for false). Rewrite needed to keep 1.4 at 9 cards. Page shows a 'jailbreak' annotation with detected true and filtered false, confirmed.
rewrite.statement: In a Foundry guardrail annotation, a user prompt attack with detected set to true means the request was blocked.
rewrite.explanation: detected only reports that Prompt Shields flagged an attack. The filtered value shows whether the guardrail blocked it; in annotate mode an attack is detected but not filtered.
rewrite.misconception: Detection of an attack implies the guardrail blocked it.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Prompt Shields in Azure AI Content Safety

rewrite.reason: weak_card (definition card). Rewrite needed to keep 1.4 at 9 cards. The example 'I want us to only talk in URL encoding' is classified as a prompt attack, and Encoding attacks is a listed subtype (confirmed). Uses 'treats ... as' on a true card, which the scan flagged as a false-only marker.
rewrite.statement: Prompt Shields treats a user's request to reply only in URL encoding as a user prompt attack.
rewrite.explanation: Encoding attacks are a user prompt attack subtype: ciphers and character transformations can slip past system rules, so requests for encoded output get flagged.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Prompt Shields in Azure AI Content Safety

rewrite.reason: source_problem: the old source and field names (codeCitations.sourceUrls) exist only in the 2024-09-15-preview standalone API. Rewritten to the GA Foundry guardrail annotation, confirmed: 'Example citation of public GitHub repository where code snippet was found; The license of the repository' and 'we strongly recommend that the application also displays the example citation'.
rewrite.statement: A Foundry guardrail's protected material code annotation can cite a public GitHub repository for matched code.
rewrite.explanation: When protected material code is detected, the annotation can carry an example GitHub repository URL and its license. Microsoft strongly recommends showing that citation with the code.
rewrite.sourceTitle: How to configure guardrails and controls in Microsoft Foundry

rewrite.reason: weak_card (name giveaway; sibling of s2.2-03). Rewrite needed to keep 2.1 at 9 cards. 'Alternatively, you can manually carry forward output items in the next request' confirmed.
rewrite.statement: Azure OpenAI v1 apps can continue a Responses API chat by resending earlier output items as input.
rewrite.explanation: Besides previous_response_id chaining, an app can append the earlier response's output items to its next input, keeping conversation state in its own code.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Use the Azure OpenAI Responses API

rewrite.reason: weak_card (RAG definition). Rewrite needed to keep 2.1 at 9 cards, and it fills the uncovered 'Foundry SDKs' bullet. 'use the OpenAI-compatible client for running agents, evaluations, and calling models' and 'project.get_openai_client()' confirmed; appliesTo azure-ai-projects 2.3.0.
rewrite.statement: With azure-ai-projects 2.3.0, an app runs Foundry evaluations through the client from get_openai_client().
rewrite.explanation: AIProjectClient handles project setup such as connections. The OpenAI-compatible client from get_openai_client() runs Responses calls, agents and evaluations.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Get started with Microsoft Foundry SDKs and endpoints

rewrite.reason: weak_card (near-truism; sibling of s2.1-02). Rewrite needed to keep 2.2 at 9 cards. 'The conversation itself is not truncated, but only a subset of it is used to generate the response' confirmed.
rewrite.statement: A Foundry Agents v2 conversation keeps its stored items when the model truncates input past its context size.
rewrite.explanation: When a conversation outgrows the model's context window, only the input sent to the model is truncated. The conversation object keeps every item for later turns.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Build with runtime components in Foundry Agent Service

rewrite.reason: weak_card (guessable wording; loose 'knowledge store'). Rewrite needed to keep 2.2 at 9 cards. Confirmed: 'Dynamic at runtime ... omit vector_store_ids ... Callers supply it in the tools/call arguments, so each call can target a different vector store'.
rewrite.statement: Omitting vector_store_ids from a Foundry toolbox's file search tool makes each tools/call name its store.
rewrite.explanation: Pinned vector_store_ids fix the store for every call. Leaving them out at toolbox creation makes callers pass store IDs in tools/call arguments, so a multitenant app searches per request.
rewrite.sourceTitle: File search tool for Microsoft Foundry agents

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: 'share tools with a Foundry agent' could mean contributing client-side function tools, which toolboxes cannot hold. Narrowed to consuming toolbox tools. Confirmed: 'Any MCP-compatible runtime or client can use a toolbox, including custom agents built with Microsoft Agent Framework, LangGraph'. The verifier's 'client-executed function tools' sentence was left out because it would give away s2.2-01.
rewrite.statement: A Microsoft Agent Framework app can use a Foundry toolbox's tools through its MCP-compatible endpoint.
rewrite.explanation: Toolboxes are Foundry-homed but not Foundry-bound: any MCP-compatible runtime or client, including Microsoft Agent Framework and LangGraph, can use one.
rewrite.sourceTitle: What is Toolbox in Microsoft Foundry?

rewrite.reason: weak_card (self-contradictory wording: 'summary' returns 'raw'). Rewrite needed to keep 2.3 at 9 cards. Confirmed: 'The reasoning items stay opaque, and the API never returns their reasoning text'. all_turns is supported by GPT-5.6 models and is their default.
rewrite.statement: A gpt-5.6-sol app reads earlier turns' reasoning text from items kept with reasoning.context set to all_turns.
rewrite.explanation: all_turns lets the model reuse earlier reasoning items, but the items stay opaque and the API never returns their text. The reasoning summary parameter gives an app a summary instead.
rewrite.misconception: Persisted reasoning items expose their reasoning text to the app.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Azure OpenAI reasoning models

rewrite.reason: tell: removes 'lets' and the engineer-subject framing on a true card. Fact (separate model-call and tool spans with their own durations) and answer unchanged; original explanation kept.
rewrite.statement: A Microsoft Foundry prompt-agent trace records model calls and tool executions as separately timed spans.
rewrite.explanation: A prompt-agent trace separates model operations from tool operations. Inspecting their spans helps an engineer locate the step responsible for a latency spike.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Agent tracing overview

rewrite.reason: weak_card (strawman). Rewrite needed to keep 2.3 at 9 cards. Confirmed: 'Tracing is off by default. No trace data is collected or stored unless explicitly enabled', 'Tracing is enabled when a project is connected to an Azure Monitor Application Insights resource', and 'The Application Insights resource connected to the Foundry project stores trace data'.
rewrite.statement: Microsoft Foundry keeps prompt-agent traces in its own project store until an engineer connects Application Insights.
rewrite.explanation: Foundry tracing is off by default: no trace data is collected until the project is connected to Azure Monitor Application Insights, which then stores the traces.
rewrite.misconception: Foundry collects traces before any telemetry resource is connected.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Microsoft Foundry tracing and data handling

rewrite.reason: weak_card (truism). Rewrite needed to keep 3.1 at 9 cards. Confirmed: 'You can provide up to 16 input images'. The explanation leaves out the PNG/JPG rule so it does not give away s3.1-08.
rewrite.statement: The app sends a product photo and a logo as two input images in one GPT-Image-2 edit call.
rewrite.explanation: The Image Edit API accepts several input images per request, up to 16 on Azure OpenAI, so the app can combine a product shot with a logo.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Azure OpenAI image generation models

rewrite.reason: weak_card (giveaway; the old REST reference omitted gpt-image-2 and listed webp). Rewrite needed to keep 3.1 at 9 cards. Confirmed on the how-to: 'Supported formats are PNG and JPEG. The default is PNG.' The statement drops the 'The app' opening that marked true cards in 3.1.
rewrite.statement: GPT-Image-2 returns PNG when the app leaves output_format out of its request.
rewrite.explanation: Azure OpenAI image generation defaults output_format to PNG, so the app receives PNG unless it requests another supported format.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Azure OpenAI image generation models

rewrite.reason: wrong_answer: OpenAI documents that gpt-image-2 does not accept a changed input_fidelity, and Azure gives no support for it. The verifier's replacement was confirmed on the Azure how-to: 'The mask must be a PNG file and have the same dimensions as the input image.' The explanation leaves out the transparent-pixel fact of s3.1-06.
rewrite.statement: The app's GPT-Image-2 edit mask is a PNG file whose dimensions match the input image.
rewrite.explanation: Azure OpenAI requires an image edit mask to be a PNG file with the same dimensions as the input image it accompanies.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Azure OpenAI image generation models

rewrite.reason: weak_card (wording giveaway, vague explanation). Rewrite needed to keep 3.1 at 9 cards. Confirmed: GPT-Image-2 takes arbitrary WIDTHxHEIGHT sizes with both edges multiples of 16 px and an aspect ratio between 1:3 and 3:1; GPT-Image-1 series uses fixed sizes 1024x1024, 1024x1536 and 1536x1024.
rewrite.statement: GPT-Image-2 limits the app's size parameter to the 1024x1024, 1024x1536 and 1536x1024 values.
rewrite.explanation: GPT-Image-2 accepts custom WIDTHxHEIGHT sizes when both edges are multiples of 16 px and the aspect ratio stays between 1:3 and 3:1. The three fixed sizes belong to GPT-Image-1 models.
rewrite.misconception: GPT-Image-2 keeps GPT-Image-1's fixed size list.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Azure OpenAI image generation models

The statement was also shortened to drop 'vision-capable models', which hinted s1.1-06, and to bring the 3.2 true/false averages within 5 characters. Fact and answer are unchanged.
rewrite.statement: Azure OpenAI v1 apps pair input_text and input_image in one Responses API message.
rewrite.explanation: A Responses API message carries the question text and the image as separate content parts, so the model reads both in one request.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Use the Azure OpenAI Responses API

cards.explanation: Code Interpreter runs in Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions placed in the Foundry project's own region, which matters when an engineer plans for data residency.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; region and dynamic-sessions sentences confirmed on the code-interpreter page.

cards.statement: An engineer selects Phi-4-mini-instruct as a small language model for captioning product photos.
cards.explanation: Phi-4-mini-instruct accepts text input only. Phi-4-multimodal-instruct is the Phi-4 option that accepts text, images and audio.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; input modalities confirmed in the models-from-partners table.

cards.statement: Microsoft suggests Global Provisioned when a region lacks PTU capacity and global data processing is acceptable.
cards.explanation: Global Provisioned reserves PTUs but may process data in any Azure region, so Microsoft offers it as a fix for missing regional PTU capacity when no geography rule requires local processing.
cards.reason: Fact lens fix adopted (wording lens had no conflicting change): the condition on global processing moves into the statement so a geography-bound expert cannot argue False. Confirmed on deployment-types: troubleshooting row 'No PTU capacity in region | Try a different region or use Global Provisioned', table 'Global Provisioned | Any Azure region | Reserved PTU', 'Keep processing within an Azure geography | Standard or Regional Provisioned'. Volatility stays may_change. 112/190 chars.

cards.statement: An app puts the catalog model name in the model parameter to call a deployment that has a custom name.
cards.explanation: During inference, the model parameter carries the deployment name. A deployment given a custom name at creation is called by that name, not by the catalog model name.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; deploy-foundry-models states the deployment name is used in the model parameter and can be changed before deploying.

cards.statement: In Foundry Agents v2, a developer who saves edited instructions for an agent creates a new agent version.
cards.explanation: Saved Foundry agent versions are immutable, so any change is saved as a new version. Code refers to an agent as <agent_name>:<version>.
cards.reason: Wording lens fix adopted: 'changes a saved agent version' contradicted immutability and invited a False answer. Confirmed on development-lifecycle: 'Each version of an agent is immutable after you save it. Any modifications to an existing version require saving and creating a new version' and '<agent_name>:<version>'. 105 chars.

cards.statement: Azure Monitor splits Azure OpenAI's blocked-request metric by the content category behind each block.
cards.explanation: The Blocked Volume metric counts Azure OpenAI requests rejected by content filters. Its Category dimension helps an engineer identify the categories causing rejections.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; fact lens minor note (Category dimension not described in words) is not a blocker.

cards.statement: An Azure AI Search indexer run can report success while some documents in that run failed to index.
cards.explanation: A run still counts as successful while its document errors stay below the indexer's Max failed items setting, so an engineer checks a run's errors even after success.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; Success row with Max failed items confirmed.

cards.statement: Foundry User on a Foundry resource gives a developer permission to publish agents from its projects.
cards.explanation: Foundry User covers building and testing agents in a project. Publishing agents needs at least Foundry Project Manager at the Foundry resource scope.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; rbac-foundry permissions table and Project Manager minimum confirmed.

cards.statement: Azure OpenAI's Time to Response metric includes network latency between the client app and the API endpoint.
cards.explanation: Time to Response is measured at the API gateway up to the first response, so client-side network latency is outside it. End-to-end timing comes from the app's own logging.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; 'as measured by the API gateway ... does not account for any client-side latency' confirmed.

cards.statement: In a Foundry guardrail annotation, a user prompt attack with detected set to true means the request was blocked.
cards.explanation: detected only reports that Prompt Shields flagged an attack. The filtered value shows whether the guardrail blocked it; in annotate mode an attack is detected but not filtered.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; detected/filtered booleans and annotate mode confirmed.

cards.statement: Prompt Shields treats a user's request to reply only in URL encoding as a user prompt attack.
cards.explanation: Encoding attacks are a user prompt attack subtype: ciphers and character transformations can slip past system rules, so requests for encoded output get flagged.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; URL encoding example and Encoding attacks subtype confirmed.

cards.statement: A Foundry guardrail's protected material code annotation can cite a public GitHub repository for matched code.
cards.explanation: When protected material code is detected, the annotation can carry an example GitHub repository URL and its license. Microsoft strongly recommends showing that citation with the code.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; GA guardrail annotation citation and recommendation confirmed.

cards.statement: Azure OpenAI v1 apps can continue a Responses API chat by resending earlier output items as input.

cards.reason: Both lenses keep; 'manually carry forward output items in the next request' confirmed.

cards.statement: With azure-ai-projects 2.3.0, an app runs Foundry evaluations through the client from get_openai_client().

cards.reason: Both lenses keep; sdk-overview split between project client and OpenAI-compatible client confirmed.

cards.statement: A Foundry Agents v2 conversation keeps its stored items when the model truncates input past its context size.
cards.explanation: When a conversation outgrows the model's context window, only the input sent to the model is truncated. The conversation object keeps every item for later turns.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep; 'The conversation itself is not truncated' confirmed.

cards.statement: If a Foundry toolbox file search tool omits vector_store_ids, its callers pass the store IDs in tools/call.
cards.explanation: Pinned vector_store_ids fix the store for every call. Leaving them out at toolbox creation makes callers pass store IDs in tools/call arguments, so a multitenant app searches per request.
cards.reason: Wording lens fix adopted (awkward phrasing, 'each' coverage-word imbalance).
